lessons.did_you_know: The East India Company began in 1600 with just 218 London merchants and a single clerk operating from a townhouse on Leadenhall Street—yet within 150 years, this private corporation commanded a private mercenary army of 260,000 soldiers, twice the size of the British Army! narrative_blocks.title: The London Charter (1600–1615)
narrative_blocks.text: [1.1] On New Year’s Eve 1600, Queen Elizabeth I granted a royal charter to the Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies. Seeking lucrative Asian spices, silk, and cotton textiles to rival Portuguese and Dutch traders, 218 wealthy London merchants pooled their capital. The Crown granted the East India Company an exclusive trade monopoly east of the Cape of Good Hope. Early voyages faced catastrophic shipwreck, scurvy, and Portuguese cannon fire, but the profits were astronomical: a single cargo of pepper or cloves could return over 300% on a merchant’s investment.

narrative_blocks.title: Coastal Fortresses & Mughal Factories (1615–1700)
narrative_blocks.text: [1.2] When English merchants arrived in India, they encountered the vast, glittering Mughal Empire, whose economy accounted for nearly a quarter of global manufacturing. In 1615, King James I dispatched Sir Thomas Roe to the court of Emperor Jahangir. Roe bowed low and secured permission to construct permanent trading posts called factories along the coastline at Surat, Madras, and Calcutta. Behind fortified walls, English company factors traded bullion for fine woven calicoes and raw silk, while training regiments of native Indian soldiers called sepoys to defend their warehouses from rival French garrisons.

source.title: Source A: Nathaniel Dance, Portrait of Major-General Robert Clive (1773)
source.caption: Major-General Robert Clive, 1st Baron Clive of Plassey, painted by Nathaniel Dance in royal red and gold military uniform, with the smoke of battle and Indian cavalry in the background.
source.source_context: Robert Clive rose from an unruly teenage clerk on a £5 annual salary to commander-in-chief of the East India Company’s armed forces, amassing a personal fortune of £300,000 through military conquest and political bribery.
source.how_useful_question: How useful is Source A for an enquiry into how British imperial commanders like Robert Clive presented their military leadership in India?
provenance_clues: Author: Nathaniel Dance, a fashionable London portraitist commissioned by wealthy British elites.
Audience: British parliamentarians, high society, and the London art establishment.
Motive: To project Clive as a heroic, aristocratic military commander defending British imperial interests, overshadowing accusations of corruption and extortion in India.
source.hinge_question: Does Dance depict Clive as a legitimate British military hero or as an agent of corporate plunder?
source.citation: Nathaniel Dance • National Portrait Gallery, London.
discussion_ideas: A Victorious Patriotic Hero of Empire: Nathaniel Dance depicts Clive standing resolute in scarlet military uniform against a dramatic backdrop of swirling battlefield smoke, with an Indian obelisk and palm trees behind him; the portrait visually frames Clive as a brilliant imperial commander who secured British supremacy at the Battle of Plassey (1757) and expanded British trade.

A Corrupt Corporate 'Nabob' Enriched by Plunder: In 1773, when Dance painted this portrait, Clive was under hostile parliamentary investigation for gross corruption, extortion, and amassing a personal fortune of over £234,000 while serving as an agent of the East India Company; critics in Parliament condemned him for corporate greed that provoked the catastrophic Great Bengal Famine of 1770, which starved ten million Indian peasants.

narrative_blocks.title: The Storm at Calcutta (1756)
narrative_blocks.text: [1.3] By the mid-18th century, the Mughal Empire was fracturing into warring regional kingdoms. Bengal was the wealthiest province in Asia, producing exquisite textiles and bountiful rice harvests. When the youthful, fiercely patriotic Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah inherited Bengal in 1756, he ordered the British to dismantle unauthorised fortifications at Fort William in Calcutta. When company officials insolently refused, Siraj marched 50,000 troops, stormed Calcutta, and captured the garrison. British propagandists seized upon the disputed "Black Hole of Calcutta"—claiming dozens of English captives suffocated in a cramped military cell—to whip up imperial vengeance in London.

narrative_blocks.title: Treachery at Plassey (June 1757)
narrative_blocks.text: [1.4] The Company dispatched Robert Clive from Madras with 3,000 troops (mostly Indian sepoys) to retake Bengal. Knowing he was vastly outnumbered by Siraj’s 50,000-strong army, Clive resorted to conspiracy. He secretly met Mir Jafar, Siraj’s disgruntled commander-in-chief, bribing him with the Bengali throne in exchange for battlefield betrayal. On 23 June 1757, the armies collided in a mango grove at Plassey. When a sudden monsoon torrential downpour soaked Siraj’s exposed gunpowder, Clive kept his own ammunition dry under canvas tarpaulins. Mir Jafar held back his regiments, Siraj’s lines collapsed, and Clive seized Bengal with fewer than 30 British casualties.

narrative_blocks.title: The Treaty of Allahabad & Corporate Plunder (1765–1770)
narrative_blocks.text: [1.5] Following further military triumphs, Clive cornered the weakened Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. In August 1765, under a silk canopy at Allahabad, the Emperor signed away the Diwani—the sovereign constitutional right to collect all land taxes across Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. Overnight, a private commercial corporation became the absolute government of 20 million people. The Company pocketed £3 million annually in tax revenue, using Bengal’s own taxes to purchase Indian goods for export to Europe. When drought struck in 1769–1770, the Company maintained ruthless tax enforcement, resulting in the Great Bengal Famine, which killed an estimated 10 million people.

source.title: Source B: Benjamin West, Shah Alam II Conveying the Grant of the Diwani to Lord Clive (1795)
source.caption: Benjamin West’s historic oil painting depicting Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II on his elevated imperial throne, formally handing the legal scroll of the Diwani to Robert Clive and company officers in August 1765.
source.source_context: The 1765 Treaty of Allahabad transformed the East India Company from a maritime trading enterprise into a sovereign territorial power with the legal right to collect taxes from 20 million Indian subjects.
source.how_useful_question: How useful is Source B for an enquiry into how the British East India Company justified its takeover of sovereign power in Bengal?
provenance_clues: Author: Benjamin West, American-born court painter to King George III, working thirty years after the event.
Audience: The British royal court, politicians, and the public viewing the painting at the Royal Academy.
Motive: To portray the British acquisition of sovereign power as an orderly, respectful, and legally legitimate diplomatic ceremony rather than a forced military shakedown.
source.hinge_question: Why did West depict this scene as a peaceful legal ceremony rather than a forced military shakedown?
source.citation: Benjamin West • British Library / Foreign and Commonwealth Office Collection, London.
discussion_ideas: Benjamin West painted this scene thirty years after the event to create an official visual myth of imperial legitimacy. In reality, Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II was a defeated, powerless captive whose forces had been routed at Buxar; he was compelled at gunpoint in an ordinary military tent to surrender the Diwani (tax collection rights) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. West replaces this forced military extortion with a neoclassical ceremonial tableau: Shah Alam sits serenely upon an elevated imperial pavilion, bestowing the treaty scroll upon a bowed, deferential Lord Clive as if granting a voluntary feudal honor. This whitewashed depiction was designed to reassure British audiences that the East India Company’s rule was not an aggressive corporate land-grab, but an orderly, legal, and civilized succession of power.

lessons.prologue: In 1600, Queen Elizabeth I granted a royal charter to a tiny syndicate of London merchants trading in Indian spices. Over 150 years, this private corporation built its own mercenary armies, forts, and warships. In 1757, Robert Clive defeated the Nawab of Bengal at Plassey. How did a commercial company become the ruler of millions?

video.title: How one of the most profitable companies in history rose to power | TED-Ed
video.teacher_guidance: Examine the unique corporate-military structure of the East India Company (EIC). Focus on its 1600 Royal Charter granting a trade monopoly, its private mercenary army (which grew to over 200,000 men, dwarfing the British Army), and how it transitioned from mercantile commerce to sovereign territorial rule following the 1765 Treaty of Allahabad.
video.viewing_task: How did the East India Company transform from an association of London spice merchants into a sovereign military power capable of collecting taxes across Bengal?
video.model_answer: Originally granted a royal monopoly in 1600 to trade spices, the EIC established fortified coastal trading factories at Surat, Madras, and Calcutta. To protect its investments against rival European powers and regional rulers, the Company built its own private standing army composed of British officers and recruited Indian soldiers (sepoys). Following Robert Clive's victory at Plassey in 1757, the EIC forced the Mughal Emperor to sign the 1765 Treaty of Allahabad, granting the Company the 'Diwani'—the legal right to collect land revenue and taxes from 20 million people in Bengal, transforming a private corporation into an imperial ruler.

video.title: How did the British gain control of India? | History - Empire | BBC Bitesize for Teachers
video.teacher_guidance: This BBC Bitesize clip analyzes how the EIC exploited the fracturing of the Mughal Empire after Emperor Aurangzeb's death. Focus on Robert Clive's conspiracy with wealthy financier Jagat Seth and military commander Mir Jafar to overthrow Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah at the Battle of Plassey in 1757.
video.viewing_task: What political divisions within Bengal did Robert Clive exploit to defeat Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah at the Battle of Plassey in 1757?
video.model_answer: Clive exploited intense internal opposition to the young Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah among Bengal's ruling elite. He formed a secret alliance with the Nawab's disaffected army commander, Mir Jafar, and wealthy Hindu banking financiers (the Jagat Seths). At Plassey, Mir Jafar kept the majority of the Nawab's cavalry and troops inactive on the battlefield in exchange for Clive's promise to install him as a puppet ruler, enabling Clive's force of just 3,000 men to rout the Nawab's 50,000-strong army.

stages.title: The Mechanics of the Triangular Trade
stages.trigger: British merchants established a vast triangular trade: carrying manufactured guns and brass to Africa, kidnapped human captives to the Americas, and raw sugar to Britain.
stages.connective: Enriched British port cities like Bristol and Liverpool, embedding colonial slavery into the core foundation of British maritime wealth.
stages.question: How did the Triangular Trade connect Britain, Africa, and the Americas?

stages.title: The Royal African Company & The Asiento
stages.actor: King Charles II & Duke of York
stages.trigger: King Charles II granted a monopoly charter to the Royal African Company, whose ships branded captives with ‘RAC’, followed by Britain securing the Spanish Asiento contract.
stages.connective: Institutionalized human trafficking under royal protection, turning Britain into the world’s preeminent transatlantic slave-trading power.
stages.question: How did royal monopolies and the Asiento expand British slaving?

stages.title: The Horrors of the Middle Passage
stages.trigger: Enslaved Africans were crammed below decks on suffocating wooden shelves, shackled in pairs with iron leg-irons while enduring lethal dysentery and extreme trauma.
stages.connective: Resulted in the deaths of over 1.5 million people during oceanic transit, treating human beings as mere perishable commercial cargo.
stages.question: What forensic conditions characterised the horrors of the Middle Passage?

stages.title: The Zong Massacre & Chattel Slavery
stages.trigger: Running low on water, Captain Luke Collingwood ordered 133 sick enslaved people thrown alive into the sea so the ship’s owners could claim £30 per head in insurance.
stages.connective: Exposed the barbaric reality of chattel slavery when London judges treated the atrocity as an ordinary commercial property insurance dispute.
stages.question: How did the Zong massacre expose the dehumanising logic of chattel slavery?

stages.title: The Brookes Diagram & Abolitionism
stages.trigger: Abolitionists published the forensic cross-section diagram of the slave ship Brookes alongside Olaudah Equiano’s bestselling autobiography detailing the terrors of enslavement.
stages.connective: Galvanized British public opinion against the trade, forcing Parliament to pass the Abolition of the Slave Trade Act in 1807.
stages.question: How did the Brookes diagram and Equiano’s voice ignite abolitionism?

lessons.did_you_know: British slave ship captains insured their human captives as literal commercial cargo, classing them in legal paperwork alongside cattle and timber! When Captain Luke Collingwood of the slave ship Zong got lost at sea in 1781 and ran low on drinking water, he ordered 133 living enslaved Africans thrown overboard into shark-infested waters to claim insurance money for "jettisoned cargo"—a legal horror that stunned the public when the insurers refused to pay and the case was fought in London courts as a commercial contract dispute!

narrative_blocks.title: The Triangular Engine (1619–1672)
narrative_blocks.text: [2.1] In 1619, a privateer vessel landed the first twenty captive Angolans in English Virginia, initiating a brutal economic nexus known as the Triangular Transatlantic Trade. On the first leg, British merchant ships departed Bristol and Liverpool loaded with manufactured guns, brass pans, alcohol, and woollen cloth. On the West African coast, these goods were bartered with local rulers and slave-raiders for captive men, women, and children. On the second leg—the dreaded Middle Passage—captives were shipped to the Caribbean and Americas. On the final leg, the ships returned to Britain packed with lucrative slave-grown raw commodities: sugar, tobacco, and cotton.

narrative_blocks.title: Capture, Barracoons & The Royal African Company (1672–1713)
narrative_blocks.text: [2.2] In 1672, King Charles II granted a royal charter to the Royal African Company, headed by his brother, the Duke of York (later James II). The Company branded captive Africans on their chests with the letters "DY" using red-hot irons. Captives had typically been kidnapped in violent inland raids, marched hundreds of miles in wooden neck-yokes to the coast, and locked in suffocating underground stone dungeons called barracoons at coastal slave fortresses like Cape Coast Castle. By 1713, Britain secured the coveted Asiento monopoly from Spain, making British merchants the undisputed rulers of the global slave trade.

narrative_blocks.title: The Agony of the Middle Passage (1713–1781)
narrative_blocks.text: [2.3] The Middle Passage took between six and twelve weeks across the Atlantic. Captains operated on "tight packing," cramming up to 600 people into dark, unventilated holds with ceiling heights under three feet. Captives were chained in pairs by their wrists and ankles, forced to lie spoon-fashioned on bare wooden planks amidst vomit, blood, and dysentery. The stench was so overpowering that sailors reported smelling a slave ship miles before sighting it. Between 12% and 15% of captives died during the voyage from dehydration, smallpox, and grief, their bodies thrown to following sharks.

source.title: Source A: The Plymouth Committee, Stowage of the British Slave Ship Brookes (1788)
source.caption: The famous 1788 abolitionist cross-section diagram of the slave ship Brookes, detailing how 454 enslaved human beings were systematically packed onto shelves like inanimate merchandise.
source.source_context: Published in London by Thomas Clarkson and the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade, this factual architectural print was distributed to Parliament, schools, and coffeehouses, becoming the most influential political poster of the 18th century.
source.how_useful_question: How useful is Source A for an enquiry into the conditions endured by enslaved Africans during the Middle Passage?
provenance_clues: Author: The Plymouth Committee of the Abolitionist Society, drawn from precise measurements taken by British naval captain William Bligh.
Audience: British MPs, voters, and the wider public who had never witnessed a slave ship.
Motive: To provide undeniable forensic proof of the systematic, calculated cruelty of the slave trade to force Parliament to pass abolition laws.
source.hinge_question: Why did abolitionists choose a technical diagram rather than an emotional painting?
source.citation: Plymouth Committee • British Library / National Maritime Museum, Greenwich.
discussion_ideas: The Plymouth Abolition Committee made the deliberate tactical decision to use an objective architectural plan because cold technical diagrams were impossible for slave traders to deny or refute as artistic exaggeration. By depicting the exact dimensions of the ship's hold and showing over 450 human bodies packed shoulder-to-shoulder in rows with each adult male allotted a space just six feet long by sixteen inches wide, the cross-section visually exposed the monstrous reality of chattel slavery: treating human beings not as persons, but as inert, tightly packed cargo. Circulated across Britain, America, and France, this unemotional blueprint stripped away the polite fictions of the slave trade and forced the public to confront the physical horror of the Middle Passage.

narrative_blocks.title: The Zong Atrocity & Captive Resistance (1781)
narrative_blocks.text: [2.4] Enslaved Africans resisted their captors at every stage. Historians have documented armed insurrections aboard over 400 slave ships; many captives staged suicidal hunger strikes or hurled themselves overboard into the sea rather than submit to lifelong bondage. The ultimate horror of the trade was exposed in 1781 aboard the British slave ship Zong. Running low on fresh water due to navigational errors, Captain Luke Collingwood ordered 133 sick and living enslaved Africans thrown into the ocean so the ship owners could collect £30 per person from their maritime insurance company for "lost cargo."

narrative_blocks.title: Olaudah Equiano & The Awakening Conscience (1788–1807)
narrative_blocks.text: [2.5] The legal aftermath of the Zong horrified British reformers like Granville Sharp and Thomas Clarkson. In 1788, the Abolition Society published the explosive Brookes diagram, visually demonstrating that human beings were stacked like books on shelves. In 1789, Olaudah Equiano, a formerly enslaved Igbo man who had purchased his freedom, published his bestselling autobiography. Equiano lectured across Britain, delivering harrowing first-person testimony about the shrieks of women and the suffocating pestilence of the hold. Equiano’s voice and the Brookes diagram ignited the mass abolition movement that culminated in the 1807 Abolition of the Slave Trade Act.

source.caption: Frontispiece engraving of Olaudah Equiano from his 1789 autobiography The Interesting Narrative: depicted as an educated Christian gentleman holding an open Bible.
source.source_context: Kidnapped from modern-day Nigeria as a boy, Equiano survived the Middle Passage, was enslaved in Virginia and the Caribbean, learned to read and write, and purchased his freedom in 1766 before becoming a prominent leader of London’s Black community.

Audience: Literate middle- and upper-class British readers, MPs, and churchgoers.
Motive: To directly disprove the pro-slavery claim that Africans were naturally uncivilised or subhuman by presenting himself as an educated, refined, and deeply moral Christian scholar.
source.hinge_question: Why did Equiano insist on European attire holding an open Bible?
source.citation: Daniel Orme • Frontispiece of The Interesting Narrative (1789).
discussion_ideas: Direct Refutation of Pro-Slavery Racial Stereotypes: Pro-slavery apologists claimed that African people were uncivilized savages who lacked the capacity for moral reasoning, education, or Christian faith; by presenting himself in elegant British gentleman's attire—a frock coat, ruffled cravat, and styled hair—holding an open Bible, Equiano visually demolished racist caricatures and asserted his full intellectual, moral, and spiritual equality.

lessons.prologue: Between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, European slave ships forcibly transported over twelve million African men, women, and children across the Atlantic Ocean. Packed in suffocating darkness below deck, captives endured the unspeakable horrors of the Middle Passage. What were the brutal economic mechanics and human costs of this global trading empire?

video.title: The Atlantic slave trade: What too few textbooks told you | TED-Ed
video.teacher_guidance: Use this TED-Ed animation by historian Anthony Hazard to deconstruct the economic machinery of the Triangular Trade. Emphasize that enslaved Africans were not merely labourers, but skilled farmers, ironworkers, and weavers whose forced labour built the transatlantic capitalist economy while decimating African societies.
video.viewing_task: How did the three legs of the Triangular Trade operate, and what lasting impact did the trade have on West African societies and British port cities?
video.model_answer: The first leg carried manufactured British goods (guns, textiles, metalware) from ports like Liverpool and Bristol to West Africa, where they were exchanged for captured African men, women, and children. The second leg (the Middle Passage) transported enslaved captives across the Atlantic under inhumane conditions to the Americas. The third leg carried slave-produced raw commodities (sugar, tobacco, cotton, rum) back to Europe. While British port cities amassed immense banking and commercial wealth that fueled the Industrial Revolution, West African societies suffered demographic collapse, intensified regional warfare driven by European firearms, and severe economic distortion.

video.title: Life Aboard a Slave Ship | HISTORY
video.teacher_guidance: This documentary explores the dehumanizing mechanics of the Middle Passage using archival ship plans (such as the famous 1788 Brookes diagram) and primary survivor accounts. Address the systematic brutalization, extreme packing, dysentery/scurvy epidemics, and the desperate acts of resistance, including shipboard insurrections and hunger strikes.
video.viewing_task: How did slave ship captains maximize their profits during the Middle Passage, and what physical and psychological brutalities did enslaved Africans endure aboard ship?
video.model_answer: Captains practiced 'tight-packing', forcing 400 to 600 human beings into suffocating holds with barely 45 centimetres of headroom, shackled in pairs by ankle irons to maximize cargo volume per voyage. Captives endured extreme heat, foul air contaminated with vomit and excrement, widespread dysentery ('bloody flux'), and brutal flogging. Suicide attempts (such as leaping overboard) and hunger strikes were met with violent force, including hot coals and the 'speculum oris' (a mechanical device used to force open jaws for feeding), with roughly 15% to 20% of enslaved people dying before reaching the Americas.

stages.title: Cromwell’s Conquest & The Birth of Maroons
stages.trigger: Oliver Cromwell launched the "Western Design" to conquer Jamaica from Spain, during which enslaved Africans escaped into the rugged, forested Blue Mountains.
stages.connective: Established independent, fortified Maroon settlements that resisted British colonial re-enslavement for over a century.
stages.question: How did Cromwell’s conquest of Jamaica birth the Maroon communities?

stages.title: Sugar Cane Monoculture & The Gang System
stages.trigger: Planters cleared Jamaica for intensive sugar monoculture, dividing enslaved labourers into rigid gangs driven by the cowhide whip and dangerous boiling houses.
stages.connective: Created an agro-industrial regime so lethal that planters found it cheaper to replace dying workers with fresh African imports than sustain them.
stages.question: Why was sugar cultivation described as an agro-industrial death machine?

stages.title: Everyday Resistance & Cultural Preservation
stages.trigger: Enslaved people fought back daily by breaking hoe handles, sabotaging machinery, feigning sickness, and preserving African spiritual traditions like Obeah and Anansi stories.
stages.connective: Maintained cultural identity and human dignity in defiance of colonial legal codes that classified them as mere chattel.
stages.question: How did enslaved labourers engage in daily sabotage and cultural survival?

stages.title: Queen Nanny & The First Maroon War
stages.trigger: Queen Nanny led the Windward Maroons, utilizing living branch camouflage, mountain ambush tactics, and the curved abeng horn to coordinate surprise attacks.
stages.connective: Humiliated British regular forces in the Blue Mountains, rendering the colonial militia incapable of conquering the interior.
stages.question: How did Queen Nanny lead the Windward Maroons to military victory?

stages.title: The 1739 Maroon Peace Treaty
stages.trigger: Exhausted by warfare, the British governor sent a white flag to negotiate the 1739 Treaty, granting the Maroons 1,500 acres of sovereign land.
stages.connective: Recognized Maroon independence as free sovereign subjects, but forced them into a tragic compromise: agreeing to capture and return future runaway slaves.
stages.question: Why was the 1739 Peace Treaty both a triumph and a painful compromise?

narrative_blocks.title: Cromwell’s Western Design (1655)
narrative_blocks.text: [3.1] In 1655, Oliver Cromwell launched his ambitious "Western Design" to wrest control of the Caribbean from Catholic Spain. An English naval expedition seized the mountainous island of Jamaica. As the Spanish defenders fled, their enslaved African servants slipped into the impenetrable interior of the Blue Mountains and Cockpit Country. Joining indigenous Taíno survivors, they formed independent, self-governing mountain communities known as Maroons (from the Spanish cimarrón, meaning wild or untamed). For over eighty years, these free African enclaves defied every British attempt to recapture them.

narrative_blocks.title: The Sugar Industrial Complex (1670–1730)
narrative_blocks.text: [3.2] Along the fertile coastal plains of Jamaica, British planters constructed a brutal agro-industrial machine powered by "White Gold"—sugar. Enslaved Africans were organised into the rigid gang system: the Great Gang cleared rocky land and cut thick cane with machetes under blistering tropical sun, driven by overseers brandishing leather whips. In steaming boiling houses, workers laboured through the night near bubbling cauldrons of molten sugar, where a slip meant amputation or scalding death. The work was so exhausting and food rations so meagre that life expectancy after arriving from Africa was under seven years.

source.title: Source A: William Clark, Slaves Cutting the Sugar Cane in Antigua (1823)
source.caption: William Clark’s British Library print showing enslaved men and women cutting tall sugar cane under the watchful eye of an armed overseer on horseback.
source.source_context: Published in London as part of Ten Views in the Island of Antigua, this print illustrates the intense physical labour demanded during the harvest season on Caribbean sugar estates.
source.how_useful_question: How useful is Source A for an enquiry into the nature of plantation labour and colonial control in the 18th-century British Caribbean?
provenance_clues: Author: William Clark, an English artist who lived on sugar plantations in Antigua for three years.
Audience: British readers and investors in London interested in colonial plantation life.

Motive: While realistically depicting the gang system, Clark sanitised the scene by showing neatly dressed workers without displaying the frequent whippings or horrific injuries common in sugar mills.
source.hinge_question: Why might an artist depict plantation labour looking orderly rather than showing the violence used to enforce work?
discussion_ideas: William Clark's print was produced for British audiences and plantation owners who wished to defend the Caribbean sugar industry against the mounting abolitionist campaign in Parliament. Clark deliberately depicts the enslaved workers in clean clothes, working at an unhurried, rhythmic pace under a bright Caribbean sky, with the overseer appearing calm rather than brandishing the cart whip. By erasing the brutal realities of plantation slavery—where enslaved men, women, and children were driven by the whip through 18-hour shifts cutting cane with razor-sharp machetes under scorching heat, suffering high mortality rates—Clark presented a sanitized, pastoral fantasy designed to convince British buyers that enslavement was a benign, orderly agricultural system.

narrative_blocks.title: Daily Sabotage & Cultural Survival (1680–1720)
narrative_blocks.text: [3.3] Enslaved people did not passively endure bondage. While armed rebellion meant torture and execution, workers constantly engaged in subtle daily resistance: breaking heavy hoes, deliberately working slowly ("playing the fool"), faking illness, and secretly poisoning planter livestock. Enslaved communities fiercely guarded their African heritage: singing call-and-response work songs, passing down Anansi spider trickster folklore, practicing Obeah spiritual healing, and holding midnight funeral dances that celebrated the return of deceased spirits to their African homeland.

narrative_blocks.title: Queen Nanny & The Windward Guerrillas (1720–1734)
narrative_blocks.text: [3.4] In the eastern Blue Mountains, resistance escalated into full-scale war. The Windward Maroons were led by an extraordinary spiritual and military strategist: Queen Nanny, an Asante woman believed to possess powerful spiritual powers. Nanny established Nanny Town, a fortified mountain haven. When British redcoat regiments marched into the mountains, Nanny’s warriors used brilliant guerrilla warfare: covering themselves in palm fronds as camouflage, sounding coded tactical warnings with the abeng horn, and rolling massive boulders down narrow ravine passes to crush advancing soldiers.

source.title: Source B: Memorial Bust of Queen Nanny of the Maroons, National Heroes Park
source.caption: Bronze memorial bust of Queen Nanny in Kingston, Jamaica: honoured as the national hero who led the Maroons to military victory against the British Empire.
source.source_context: Queen Nanny commanded the Windward Maroons throughout the First Maroon War (1720–1739), defeating repeated British military expeditions sent to destroy her mountain sanctuary.
source.how_useful_question: How useful is Source B for an enquiry into how modern Jamaicans commemorate 18th-century anti-colonial resistance?
provenance_clues: Author: Modern Jamaican sculptors commissioned by the Jamaican government.
Audience: Citizens of Jamaica, schoolchildren, and international visitors.
Motive: To celebrate Queen Nanny as a courageous military commander and founding mother of Jamaican freedom who outfought the British imperial army.
source.hinge_question: How does commemorating Queen Nanny challenge narratives of enslaved people as passive victims?
discussion_ideas: Celebrating Active, Militant Indigenous Resistance: Queen Nanny was the spiritual and military leader of the Windward Maroons in the Blue Mountains of Jamaica; rather than submitting to slavery, she organized escaped captives into disciplined guerrilla units who used mountain topography, camouflage, and ambushes to defeat British redcoat regiments, forcing the British Crown to sign a formal peace treaty in 1739 granting the Maroons land autonomy.

Subverting Colonial Historical Erasure: Traditional colonial histories depicted enslaved Africans as helpless victims waiting for benevolent white British politicians to liberate them; honoring Queen Nanny as Jamaica's only National Heroine recenters the historical narrative on Black agency, proving that enslaved people fought heroically for their own freedom decades before parliamentary abolition.

narrative_blocks.title: The 1739 Peace Treaty: Triumph and Compromise (1739–1740)
narrative_blocks.text: [3.5] By 1738, the British colonial government was on the brink of bankruptcy, having spent over £250,000 trying and failing to subdue the Maroons. In March 1739, Governor Edward Trelawny sent emissaries carrying a white flag to negotiate a formal treaty with Leeward Maroon leader Cudjoe, followed by a separate treaty with Queen Nanny’s Windward Maroons. The British Crown granted the Maroons 1,500 acres of sovereign land, complete tax exemption, and total self-governing autonomy. However, the treaty contained a tragic compromise: to maintain their freedom, the Maroons were forced to agree to capture and return future runaway slaves to British plantations.

tasks.title: Question 3(b) & 3(c): Contrasting Interpretations [8 marks • 10 mins]
tasks.text: Explain how Interpretations 1 and 2 differ on the nature of enslaved African resistance, and suggest one reason why they differ on the reality of plantation control. [8 marks]

interp1.title: Interpretation 1
interp1.author: Planter Edward Long, History of Jamaica (1774)
interp1.text: “The plantation negroes are naturally indolent and require the perpetual surveillance and discipline of the driver’s whip to extract labour. Without European mastery, order would instantly dissolve into ruin.”

interp2.title: Interpretation 2
interp2.author: Historian Hilary Beckles, Caribbean Freedom (2004)
interp2.text: “Enslaved Africans waged an unrelenting war of resistance through daily sabotage, spiritual preservation, and armed guerrilla struggle. Queen Nanny proved that African military strategy could humble the British imperial army.”

matrix.text: Contrast the main arguments: Long depicts enslaved Africans as passive and dependent on European control, whereas Beckles emphasizes continuous, organized resistance and strategic military defiance.

Explain why they differ: Long focuses primarily on planter disciplinary mechanisms and justifying colonial control, whereas Beckles focuses on enslaved agency, daily resistance, and Maroon guerrilla victories.
Evaluate which interpretation provides a more historically rigorous analysis of Caribbean plantation realities.

connectives: In sharp contrast, Interpretation 2 suggests that...
One reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 differ is because they have a different focus...
In contrast, Interpretation 2 focuses more on...
As a result, the authors reach different conclusions because...
tasks.model_answer:
Part B (Difference between Interpretations):
Interpretations 1 and 2 differ fundamentally over the nature of enslaved African resistance and plantation control.

Interpretation 1 portrays enslaved people as passive, claiming that order and labour were solely maintained through European surveillance and discipline. In sharp contrast, Interpretation 2 argues that enslaved Africans engaged in an unrelenting, active struggle against slavery through cultural preservation, sabotage, and armed guerrilla warfare.

Part C (Reason Why Interpretations Differ):
A primary reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 differ is that the authors have a different focus. Interpretation 1 focuses primarily on the planters' mechanisms of colonial surveillance, viewing plantation life through the disciplinary framework of the slave-owners. In contrast, Interpretation 2 focuses primarily on African resistance, agency, and military strategy, highlighting Queen Nanny and the Maroons' victories against the British imperial army. Because the authors focus on entirely different aspects of the plantation system (planter control mechanisms versus enslaved resistance and rebellion), they reach opposing conclusions.

lessons.prologue: On Caribbean sugar plantations, enslaved Africans endured backbreaking labour under the overseer's whip to feed Britain's booming sweet tooth. Yet resistance was relentless. In the misty Blue Mountains of Jamaica, Queen Nanny led runaway Maroons in daring guerrilla warfare against British soldiers. How did enslaved people actively resist colonial bondage?

video.title: The Real Story of Nanny of the Maroons | Jamaica History
video.teacher_guidance: Focus on Queen Nanny of the Windward Maroons as a master military strategist and spiritual leader. Examine how Jamaican Maroons utilized deep geographic knowledge of the mountainous Cockpit Country and Blue Mountains to conduct successful guerrilla warfare against British colonial troops.
video.viewing_task: What guerrilla warfare strategies did Queen Nanny and the Windward Maroons use to defeat heavily armed British redcoat regiments in Jamaica?
video.model_answer: Queen Nanny and her fighters exploited the rugged, dense terrain of the Blue Mountains using sophisticated camouflage—attaching branches and leaves to blend seamlessly into the forest canopy. They lured British redcoat columns into narrow mountain defiles and launched sudden ambush attacks from higher ground. Furthermore, the Maroons maintained an early warning communication network using the 'abeng' (a hollowed-out cow horn blown through a side hole) to transmit tactical signals across valleys, cutting British supply lines and causing immense casualties without engaging in open field combat.

video.title: The Voice of a Maroon: The Story of Nanny of the Maroons | Jamaica Information Service
video.teacher_guidance: Produced by the Jamaica Information Service, this brief piece explains the legal and constitutional significance of the 1739–1740 peace treaties between the British Crown and the Maroons, which recognized Maroon independence a century before the abolition of slavery.
video.viewing_task: Why was the British Crown forced to sign peace treaties with the Jamaican Maroons in 1739–1740, and what rights did the Maroons secure?
video.model_answer: After decades of costly warfare (the First Maroon War) in which British regiments repeatedly failed to conquer the mountain settlements, colonial authorities recognized that the Maroons could not be militarily defeated. The 1739–1740 treaties formally recognized Maroon sovereignty, granting them 1,500 acres of autonomous crown land, the right to govern themselves under their own chiefs (like Cudjoe and Nanny), and freedom from enslavement, making them the first legally recognized free Black communities in the colonial Americas.

narrative_blocks.title: Victory & The Debt Trap (1763)
narrative_blocks.text: [4.1] In 1763, Britain celebrated complete victory over France in the Seven Years’ War, driving French armies out of Canada and expanding the British Empire to unprecedented heights. But imperial glory carried an astronomical financial price tag: Britain’s national debt had skyrocketed to £133 million. In London, Prime Minister George Grenville argued that since British soldiers had bled to defend the American colonists, the colonists should pay taxes toward their own military defence. To prevent expensive frontier wars with Native American confederacies, King George III issued the Proclamation Line of 1763, forbidding colonists from settling west of the Appalachian Mountains—infuriating land-hungry colonial frontiersmen.

narrative_blocks.title: The Stamp Act & "No Taxation Without Representation" (1765–1766)
narrative_blocks.text: [4.2] In March 1765, Parliament passed the fateful Stamp Act, imposing the first-ever direct internal tax on the Thirteen Colonies. Every legal contract, newspaper, almanac, pamphlet, and deck of playing cards required an official embossed tax stamp. Colonists erupted in outrage. Citing the 1689 English Bill of Rights, colonial assemblies declared that as British subjects, they could only be taxed by their own elected representatives: "No taxation without representation!" In Boston, a secretive resistance movement called the Sons of Liberty formed, hanging tax collectors in effigy, ransacking the royal governor’s mansion, and organizing a nationwide boycott of British imported goods. Stunned by the collapse in British exports, Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766.

narrative_blocks.title: Blood on King Street: The Boston Massacre (March 1770)
narrative_blocks.text: [4.3] Despite repealing the Stamp Act, Parliament insisted on its absolute right to bind the colonies "in all cases whatsoever." In 1767, Chancellor Charles Townshend imposed new customs duties on imported glass, lead, paint, paper, and tea. When Bostonians violently intimidated customs officials, Britain dispatched four regiments of redcoats to occupy the city. Tensions exploded on 5 March 1770: an angry mob of dockworkers pelted a British sentry with snowballs, oyster shells, and clubs outside the Custom House. Surrounded and panicked, British soldiers fired into the crowd, killing five civilians, including Crispus Attucks, a sailor of mixed African and Native American descent. Silversmith Paul Revere engraved an explosive piece of political propaganda titled The Bloody Massacre, portraying the redcoats as cold-blooded murderers.

source.title: Source A: Paul Revere, The Bloody Massacre in King-Street (March 1770)
source.caption: Paul Revere’s famous hand-coloured copperplate engraving of the Boston Massacre: British soldiers in an organised firing squad blasting musket volleys into unarmed citizens outside "Butcher’s Hall."
source.source_context: Produced within three weeks of the 5 March 1770 incident, Revere copied Henry Pelham’s drawing to produce thousands of cheap prints distributed throughout the colonies to inflame anti-British sentiment.
source.how_useful_question: How useful is Source A for an enquiry into how colonial patriots used the Boston Massacre to build support for rebellion against British rule?
provenance_clues: Author: Paul Revere, a leading Boston silversmith and prominent member of the radical Sons of Liberty.
Audience: American colonists across all thirteen colonies, designed to be hung in taverns, parlours, and shops.
Motive: To generate explosive anti-British outrage by depicting a tragic, chaotic street brawl as a deliberate, pre-meditated military massacre ordered by Captain Preston.
source.hinge_question: What visual details in Revere’s engraving deliberately distort the reality of a chaotic street brawl?
source.citation: Paul Revere • Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington D.C.
discussion_ideas: Paul Revere's famous engraving is one of the most effective pieces of political propaganda in American history. In reality, on 5 March 1770, a small, terrified British sentry was surrounded by an angry Boston mob throwing ice, rocks, and clubs before a confused musket discharge killed five civilians. Revere deliberately altered every key detail: he depicts British Captain Preston standing behind his men with a raised sword explicitly commanding an orderly firing squad to shoot into an innocent, peaceful crowd of gentlemen; he erased all stones, snowballs, and weapons, added the label 'Butcher's Hall' above the British customs house, and added a musket firing from a civilian window, transforming a chaotic, self-defense riot into an act of cold-blooded, pre-planned military tyranny to inflame anti-British colonial fury.

narrative_blocks.title: The Tea Act & The Monopoly Threat (May 1773)
narrative_blocks.text: [4.4] Following the massacre, Parliament backed down and repealed all Townshend duties—except for a symbolic three-penny duty on tea to assert royal authority. For three years, uneasy peace held as colonists happily drank cheap Dutch smuggled tea. But in May 1773, Parliament made a disastrous blunder: the Tea Act. Seeking to bail out the bankrupt East India Company, which had 18 million pounds of unsold tea rotting in London warehouses, Parliament granted the Company a total monopoly to ship tea directly to America without paying British export tariffs. Even with the three-penny tax, Company tea was cheaper than smuggled Dutch tea. But colonial merchants and patriots saw a deadly precedent: if Parliament could grant a monopoly on tea, it could grant monopolies on bread, cloth, and iron, destroying colonial commerce.

narrative_blocks.title: 342 Chests in the Harbour: The Boston Tea Party (December 1773)
narrative_blocks.text: [4.5] In late autumn 1773, three East India Company ships—the Dartmouth, the Eleanor, and the Beaver—arrived in Boston Harbour carrying 342 chests of tea. Royal Governor Thomas Hutchinson refused to let the ships depart without paying the customs tax. On the freezing night of 16 December 1773, following an impassioned town meeting led by Samuel Adams at Old South Meeting House, over a hundred Sons of Liberty disguised themselves as Mohawk warriors. Brandishing tomahawks, they boarded the three vessels, split open all 342 wooden chests, and dumped 46 tons of East India Company tea into the ocean—worth over £1.5 million in modern money. Furious at what King George III called "flagrant rebellion," Parliament retaliated in 1774 with the Coercive Acts, closing Boston Harbour and placing Massachusetts under military dictatorship, setting the stage for war.

source.hinge_question: Why did the protestors disguise themselves as Mohawk warriors rather than performing the action as ordinary British townsfolk?

discussion_ideas: Protection from Arrest and Hanging for High Treason: Destroying 342 chests of British East India Company tea worth over £9,000 (millions today) was a felony capital crime against the Crown; donning Native American blankets, smearing soot on their faces, and communicating with mock war cries concealed the identities of prominent Sons of Liberty (including merchant smugglers) from British customs informants and royal courts.

video.teacher_guidance: Historian Ben Labaree explains the economic and constitutional tensions behind the 1773 Boston Tea Party. video.viewing_task: Why did the 1773 Tea Act outrage American colonists even though it made British East India Company tea cheaper than smuggled Dutch tea?
video.model_answer: Colonists objected because the Tea Act granted the struggling East India Company a direct commercial monopoly in North America, undercutting local colonial merchants and smugglers. More importantly, colonists recognized the act as a constitutional trap: purchasing the tea meant paying the remaining Townshend duty, thereby accepting Parliament's legal authority to levy taxes on the colonies without their consent ('no taxation without representation').

video.viewing_task: How did the Sons of Liberty execute the Boston Tea Party, and how did the British government respond to the destruction of the tea?
video.model_answer: On the night of 16 December 1773, roughly 60 members of the Sons of Liberty disguised themselves as Mohawk warriors, boarded three merchant ships (the Dartmouth, Eleanor, and Beaver) in Boston Harbor, and smashed open 342 chests of East India Company tea, dumping 45 tons of tea worth millions in modern currency into the water. King George III and Parliament retaliated in 1774 with the Coercive ('Intolerable') Acts: closing Boston Harbor, suspending Massachusetts' colonial charter, and quartering British troops in private homes, which united the Thirteen Colonies in resistance.

narrative_blocks.title: The Shot Heard ’Round the World (April–November 1775)
narrative_blocks.text: [5.1] In April 1775, British troops marched toward Concord, Massachusetts, to seize colonial weapons caches. At Lexington Green, an unknown gun fired "the shot heard ’round the world," triggering open warfare. The Continental Congress named George Washington commander-in-chief of the newly formed Continental Army. In November 1775, desperate to suppress the rebellion in Virginia, Royal Governor Lord Dunmore issued a revolutionary proclamation: he offered immediate emancipation to any enslaved African owned by rebel masters who fled and enlisted in the King’s army. Dunmore formed the "Ethiopian Regiment," where former slaves wore uniforms stitched with the motto "Liberty to Slaves."

narrative_blocks.title: The 1776 Declaration & The Paradox of Liberty (July 1776)
narrative_blocks.text: [5.2] On 4 July 1776 in Philadelphia, the Continental Congress ratified the Declaration of Independence. Authored by 33-year-old Virginian lawyer Thomas Jefferson, the document declared that "all men are created equal" with inalienable rights to "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness." Yet this ringing Enlightenment rhetoric exposed profound imperial hypocrisy: Jefferson personally owned over 170 enslaved human beings, and 41 of the 56 signatories were slaveholders. In London, the famous writer Dr Samuel Johnson sarcastically asked: "How is it that we hear the loudest yelps for liberty among the drivers of negroes?"

source.title: Source A: John Trumbull, Declaration of Independence (1819)
source.caption: John Trumbull’s celebrated oil painting in the U.S. Capitol Rotunda, showing the five-man drafting committee (including John Adams, Roger Sherman, Robert Livingston, Thomas Jefferson, and Benjamin Franklin) presenting the draft Declaration to John Hancock.
source.source_context: Commissioned by Congress decades after the Revolution, Trumbull spent years gathering authentic portraits of 42 signers to immortalise the founding of the American Republic.
source.how_useful_question: How useful is Source A for an enquiry into how early American leaders wished the Declaration of Independence to be remembered by posterity?
provenance_clues: Author: John Trumbull, former aide-de-camp to General George Washington and official artist of the American Revolution.
Audience: Citizens of the young United States and visitors to the Capitol Rotunda in Washington D.C.

Motive: To portray the founders as dignified, united, and visionary philosophers creating a republic based on universal equality, while deliberately omitting the presence of enslaved people whose labour built their estates.
source.hinge_question: Why did Trumbull omit the intense debates over slavery that nearly broke the Congress apart?
source.citation: John Trumbull • United States Capitol Rotunda, Washington D.C.
discussion_ideas: John Trumbull painted this iconic scene for the US Capitol Rotunda decades after 1776 to create a myth of unanimous, harmonious founding unity. In reality, the drafting committee (led by Thomas Jefferson) was bitterly divided: Jefferson’s original draft contained a passionate clause condemning King George III for waging 'cruel war against human nature itself' by maintaining the transatlantic slave trade. Delegates from Georgia and South Carolina furiously refused to sign unless this passage was completely excised, threatening to walk out and collapse the revolution. Trumbull erased this foundational hypocrisy, depicting 47 founding fathers standing in dignified harmony, concealing the tragic paradox that an empire of liberty was founded by slaveholders proclaiming 'all men are created equal' while keeping 500,000 Black human beings in chattel bondage.

narrative_blocks.title: Global Conflict & The French Alliance (1777–1780)
narrative_blocks.text: [5.3] The British Army was professional, well-drilled, and backed by the Royal Navy, repeatedly driving Washington’s inexperienced forces across New York and New Jersey. However, in October 1777, British General John Burgoyne was surrounded and forced to surrender his entire 6,000-man army in the forests of Saratoga, New York. Sensing British weakness, King Louis XVI of France formed a military alliance with the American rebels, followed by Spain and the Dutch Republic. What had begun as a localized colonial rebellion expanded into a global naval war, forcing Britain to divert ships and troops to defend its wealthy sugar islands in the Caribbean and factories in India.

narrative_blocks.title: Siege of Yorktown & British Surrender (October 1781)
narrative_blocks.text: [5.4] Britain pivoted its military strategy to the American South, hoping loyalist sentiment among southern planters would restore royal authority. But British General Charles Cornwallis found himself harassed by colonial guerrilla fighters and overextended. In September 1781, Cornwallis marched his 8,000 troops onto the Yorktown peninsula in Virginia, expecting Royal Navy resupply. Instead, a French fleet under Admiral de Grasse blockaded Chesapeake Bay, while combined American and French armies under Washington besieged Yorktown by land. Cut off from food and ammunition, Cornwallis surrendered on 19 October 1781. As the British troops marched out to lay down their muskets, British military bands bitterly played the tune The World Turned Upside Down.

narrative_blocks.title: The Treaty of Paris & The Black Loyalists (1783)
narrative_blocks.text: [5.5] In the 1783 Treaty of Paris, Great Britain formally recognised the independence of the United States of America, ceding all imperial territory between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mississippi River. The First British Empire had suffered catastrophic fracture. Despite furious demands from American slaveholders (including George Washington) that escaped slaves be returned, British commanders honourably kept their pledge to the Black Loyalists. In the spring of 1783, British ships evacuated over 3,000 formerly enslaved men, women, and children from New York to Nova Scotia, recording their names in the historic Book of Negroes, while thousands more resettled in London and Sierra Leone.

source.title: Source B: Excerpt from Lord Dunmore’s Proclamation, Williamsburg, Virginia (November 1775)
source.caption: Archival text of Lord Dunmore’s revolutionary proclamation offering immediate freedom to enslaved Africans who deserted rebel plantations to fight for the British Crown.
source.source_context: Issued on 7 November 1775 by John Murray, 4th Earl of Dunmore, the royal governor of Virginia, this proclamation was the first mass emancipation of enslaved Africans in American history.
source.text: "...And I do hereby further declare all indented Servants, Negroes, or others, (appertaining to Rebels,) free that are able and willing to bear Arms, they joining His MAJESTY’S Troops as soon as may be, for the more speedily reducing this Colony to a proper Sense of their Duty, to His MAJESTY’S Crown and Dignity."
source.how_useful_question: How useful is Source B for an enquiry into British military strategy and the motivations of enslaved Africans during the American Revolution?
provenance_clues: Author: Lord Dunmore, British Royal Governor of Virginia, writing from aboard a British warship after being driven from the governor’s palace.
Audience: Enslaved African Americans and rebel plantation owners across Virginia and Maryland.
Motive: Primarily military and economic—to cripple the rebel plantation economy and terrorise slaveholding rebels by arming their former enslaved workers.
source.hinge_question: Was Dunmore motivated by moral abolition or ruthless military strategy?
source.citation: Lord Dunmore • The Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History, New York.
discussion_ideas: Ruthless Military Warfare to Crush the Rebellion: Lord Dunmore was himself a wealthy slaveowner; his November 1775 proclamation offering freedom to 'all indentured servants, Negroes, or others... able and willing to bear arms' was a desperate tactical weapon designed to cripple the Virginia plantation economy and recruit an 'Ethiopian Regiment' of 800 soldiers to save his beleaguered royal garrison.

The Inadvertent Spark for Black Liberation and Loyalism: Regardless of Dunmore's cynical imperial motives, thousands of enslaved men, women, and children seized the opportunity to escape bondage and run to the British lines; known as the Black Loyalists, over 3,000 were subsequently evacuated by the British to Nova Scotia in 1783 (recorded in the Book of Negroes), transforming a British war measure into the largest emancipation of enslaved people in North America prior to the Civil War.

Audience: Citizens of the United States and visitors to the Capitol Rotunda.
Motive: To portray the founders as dignified philosophers creating a republic based on equality.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Trumbull omit the intense debates over slavery that nearly broke the Congress apart?
sources.citation: John Trumbull • United States Capitol Rotunda, Washington D.C.
discussion_ideas: John Trumbull painted this iconic scene for the US Capitol Rotunda decades after 1776 to create a myth of unanimous, harmonious founding unity. In reality, the drafting committee (led by Thomas Jefferson) was bitterly divided: Jefferson’s original draft contained a passionate clause condemning King George III for waging 'cruel war against human nature itself' by maintaining the transatlantic slave trade. Delegates from Georgia and South Carolina furiously refused to sign unless this passage was completely excised, threatening to walk out and collapse the revolution. Trumbull erased this foundational hypocrisy, depicting 47 founding fathers standing in dignified harmony, concealing the tragic paradox that an empire of liberty was founded by slaveholders proclaiming 'all men are created equal' while keeping 500,000 Black human beings in chattel bondage.

teacher_notes.primer: This synoptic capstone enquiry investigates the climax and fracture of the First British Empire. Students evaluate the outbreak of armed rebellion at Lexington, deconstruct the Enlightenment principles of the 1776 Declaration alongside the painful reality of chattel slavery, analyse how French intervention and the siege of Yorktown led to British defeat, and examine the experiences of the Black Loyalists who gained freedom fighting for the Crown.

lessons.prologue: In July 1776, American delegates proclaimed that 'all men are created equal' and declared independence from King George III. Yet thousands of enslaved Black Loyalists fled to British battle-lines, seeking genuine personal freedom under the Crown. At Yorktown in 1781, Britain surrendered. How did revolutionary ideals collide with imperial defeat and the reality of slavery?

video.title: What you might not know about the Declaration of Independence | TED-Ed
video.teacher_guidance: Kenneth C. Davis examines the philosophical rhetoric versus the human contradictions of the 1776 Declaration of Independence. Highlight Thomas Jefferson's famous assertion that 'all men are created equal' alongside the fact that Jefferson and 40 other signers enslaved over 200 people each, and examine why a draft paragraph blaming King George for the slave trade was deleted.
video.viewing_task: What central contradiction existed between the revolutionary ideals expressed in the 1776 Declaration of Independence and the socio-economic reality of the American colonies?
video.model_answer: The Declaration boldly proclaimed as 'self-evident' that 'all men are created equal' with unalienable rights to 'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness'. However, this universal philosophy was denied to roughly 500,000 enslaved African Americans who constituted one-fifth of the colonial population. Principal author Thomas Jefferson and one-third of the continental delegates were wealthy slaveholders who struck out draft condemnations of the slave trade to preserve southern economic support for the rebellion, establishing a new nation founded on freedom for white property owners while legally entrenching chattel slavery.

video.title: Who Were the Black Loyalists? | Black Loyalist Heritage Centre
video.teacher_guidance: Produced by the Black Loyalist Heritage Centre in Nova Scotia, this video explores Lord Dunmore's 1775 Proclamation and the Philipsburg Proclamation (1779). Discuss why up to 20,000 enslaved Black Americans risked their lives to escape Patriot masters and fight for the British Crown in exchange for freedom, and track their postwar evacuation to Nova Scotia, London, and Sierra Leone.
video.viewing_task: Why did thousands of enslaved African Americans choose to fight for the British Crown during the American War of Independence, and what happened to them after the British defeat in 1783?
video.model_answer: Enslaved men and women joined the British because royal governors like Lord Dunmore issued proclamations promising immediate emancipation to any enslaved person owned by rebel Patriots who joined British armed forces. Serving as soldiers (the 'Ethiopian Regiment'), guides, and labourers, over 3,000 Black Loyalists were registered in the British military's 'Book of Negroes' upon Britain's defeat in 1783, granting them official certificates of freedom and evacuating them aboard British ships to Birchtown, Nova Scotia, London, and later Freetown, Sierra Leone.
